paragraphs.heading: A particle's own angular momentum
paragraphs.text: Spin is a form of angular momentum that belongs to a particle itself. Elementary particles carry it, and so do particles built from them, such as hadrons, atomic nuclei and atoms. Spin is quantized, meaning it takes only certain separate values, and describing its interactions accurately needs relativistic quantum mechanics or quantum field theory. It is measured in the same units as ordinary angular momentum, such as J·s.

paragraphs.heading: How we know it is there
paragraphs.text: We know electron spin exists because of experiments like the one by Stern and Gerlach. There, silver atoms showed two distinct angular momenta, even though they had no orbital angular momentum. The spin–statistics theorem ties spin to the Pauli exclusion principle: seeing exclusion implies half-integer spin, and seeing half-integer spin implies exclusion.

paragraphs.heading: Counting spin
paragraphs.text: Every elementary particle of a given kind has the same size of spin, though its direction can change. That size is given by a spin quantum number. In practice, the spin angular momentum is divided by the reduced Planck constant ħ to give a plain number with no units, and this number is often just called "spin". For some particles, such as photons, spin is described as a vector. For others, such as electrons, it is a spinor, which has a size and changes under rotation like a vector but uses an unusual kind of direction.

paragraphs.heading: Not a spinning ball
paragraphs.text: The first models pictured the electron as a charged ball rotating on an axis, as the everyday word suggests. That picture breaks down when examined closely. The charge would have to be spread in a way that does not fit limits on the electron's radius, and it would have to turn faster than light. In the Standard Model, basic particles are treated as points that act through the field around them, so turning on their own axis is not well-defined. The names from these mechanical pictures have stayed, but the explanation has not.

paragraphs.heading: Pauli's abstract view
paragraphs.text: Wolfgang Pauli at first refused to link the new quantity he introduced with rotation, calling it a two-valuedness that classical physics cannot describe. Later he accepted a link to angular momentum but still treated spin as an abstract property. That stance let him prove his exclusion principle, in what is now called the spin-statistics theorem. Looking back, it helped open the modern era of particle physics, where abstract properties drawn from symmetry lead and concrete pictures are secondary.

paragraphs.heading: Steps, not slopes
paragraphs.text: Spin can also be seen as a property of waves. Hans Ohanian argued that it comes from charge flowing in circles within the electron's wave field, and a similar idea applies to water waves, where water particles move in circles smaller than a wavelength. Classical waves allow any amount of angular momentum, but quantum wave fields allow only separate values. So energy moves into or out of spin states in fixed steps. For many purposes, physicists can simply talk of integer or half-integer spin.
